analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to prove chemicals are safe before they can be sold, and forces quick action on asbestos.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2015, sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never received a committee or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the nation's main toxic chemicals law. It would require the EPA to determine, before a chemical is sold or stays on the market, that it will cause no harm to people — including children, pregnant women, workers, and the elderly — without weighing the cost of protecting them. Chemicals that can't meet that standard would have to be restricted or banned, all forms of asbestos would get a mandatory safety review within two years, manufacturers would pay fees to cover the EPA's work, and communities investigating cancer clusters would get federal help. It never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to industrial chemicals: the bill would require safety proof for chemicals in products, homes, workplaces, and drinking water, protect susceptible groups like children and pregnant women specifically, and create disease cluster investigation centers for communities facing unusual concentrations of illness.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a safety standard that ensures with reasonable certainty no harm to health or the environment, expressly excluding cost or other non-risk factors from that determination [S2] [S3].

Requires the EPA to review and act on the most dangerous chemicals on deadlines, including listing all forms of asbestos as high priority and completing an asbestos safety determination within two years and a rule within three [S2] [S3].
Blocks new chemicals and significant new uses from manufacture if the EPA finds they are not likely to meet the safety standard, instead of allowing them on the market by default [S2] [S3].

Creates Regional Disease Cluster Information and Response Centers and teams, with grants to help communities investigate disease clusters, and requires manufacturers to substantiate secrecy claims about chemical information so the EPA and public can review it [S2].
Explicitly preserves state chemical safety programs and common-law rights to sue, rather than replacing them with a single federal standard [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and processors, who would bear the cost of testing chemicals they want to sell, pay user fees to fund EPA reviews, and face restrictions, phase-outs, or bans on chemicals that cannot meet the safety standard. Some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers in product prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges some costs: for rules affecting more than $100 million a year, the EPA must analyze costs and benefits of its chosen restriction and of safer alternatives, and it may exempt uses where compliance would seriously disrupt the national economy or where no safer alternative exists [S3].

A cost-blind safety standard could force the removal of chemicals that are risky but serve uses for which no adequate substitute exists, raising prices for products from cars to electronics while the exemptions process works through those cases.

The bill's aggressive deadlines (a first list of high-priority chemicals within six months, ongoing annual lists, two-year assessments) would demand a large expansion of EPA capacity, funded by industry fees that could be challenged or lobbied down [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and direct: the current Toxic Substances Control Act has allowed most chemicals in commerce to remain unreviewed, and this bill would flip the default so industry must show safety rather than the government prove danger. The honest costs are compliance and testing expenses, some passed to consumers, plus the risk of supply disruptions for hard-to-replace chemicals — though the bill itself builds in cost analysis and exemption valves for exactly those cases. The bill is aggressive by design; its speed and cost-blindness are its main design risks, not hidden ones.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there, without a hearing, markup, or vote, until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 12, 2015 by Senator Boxer with Senators Markey and Sanders, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works that same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
The five cosponsors were four Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The complete action history shows no further action after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 114th Congress [S5].

Congress did enact TSCA reform in this period, but through a different, less stringent bill: the Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety for the 21st Century Act (S. 697), which passed the Senate unanimously and was signed into law in June 2016. That law allows the EPA to weigh costs when choosing how to regulate an unsafe chemical, uses an 'unreasonable risk' standard rather than a no-harm standard, and made the industry-funded fee framework part of the final deal.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers came out ahead: the bill that would have required a no-harm standard, cost-blind safety determinations, and mandatory asbestos deadlines died without a vote, and the competing Lautenberg Act that passed instead let the EPA weigh costs in choosing restrictions and spread deadlines over many years.

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-CA); bill sponsor and Ranking Member of the Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited Senators Markey and Sanders as original cosponsors [S1] [S3].

against.name: Jim Inhofe
against.role: Chairman, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; the committee's TSCA effort instead went to the competing Vitter-Udall bill, which became the Lautenberg Act.

against.name: Chemical manufacturing industry
against.role: Manufacturers and processors regulated under the Toxic Substances Control Act
against.what_they_did: Backed the competing Lautenberg Act framework, which unlike this bill allows cost considerations in choosing restrictions and was ultimately enacted.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Republican cosponsored this version, while the competing TSCA reform bill that eventually passed the Senate drew votes from both parties.

industries.note: The bill flips the burden of proof: companies would have to show their chemicals cause no harm, pay fees covering EPA reviews, submit to testing orders, and accept restrictions or phase-outs for chemicals that fail. Its interest ran against the bill's public health protections, and the industry got a weaker law instead.

The bill mandates that all forms of asbestos be treated as one high-priority chemical, with a safety determination due within two years and a final rule within three — a direct path to restrictions or a phase-out.

industries.industry: Independent testing laboratories and toxicology consultants
industries.note: Mandatory testing requirements, prioritization screening of hundreds of chemicals, and alternative test method development would create a large, sustained market for chemical safety testing.
